newsitem.title: USA: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) Oct 31.
newsitem.headline: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) Oct 31.

text.p: U.S. global fund managers leaned toward domestic credit markets over the past two months as they embraced relatively attractive yields here, according to a Reuters survey of fund managers and strategists.
Debt fund managers increased their bet on U.S. bonds to 24 percent of assets in October from 20 percent in August, the survey said.
"The U.S. (bond market) has become a high-yielding market," said Adam Greshin, lead portfolio manager of Scudder, Stevens and Clark global bond fund.
He said U.S portfolio managers have little incentive to own foreign bonds when they can get comparable yields in the U.S. market without the added risk of currency fluctuations.
The 10-year Treasury yield, for example, lies around 6.40 percent in the U.S. and below 6 percent or just at 6 percent in Germany and France, said Gershin.
In addition, the economic cycle appears to be shifting away from the United States and in favor of Europe and Japan.
"At this particular point in the cycle, it is now possible to project a more moderate growth path in the U.S. and a more dynamic growth path in both Europe and Japan," added Gershin.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Department reported U.S. gross domestic product grew at an annual rate of 2.2 percent in the the third quarter, less than half the 4.7 percent rate seen in the second quarter.
Economists said easing consumption, exports and government spending anchored the preliminary reading, but inventory building buoyed it above the market's expectations.

Debt portfolio managers culled funds from Germany to spread them into Japan and other European markets as well as the U.S., according to the survey. Germany, which had 16 percent of total assets in August, had 11 percent in October.

"Our view of the German market now is that it really isn't going to go anywhere," said Brian Gendreau, international market strategist at J.P. Morgan, who reduced his holdings in Germany from 39 percent in August to nil in October.
Gendreau said the Bundesbank is likely to keep rates on hold, "so why not put money to work in markets where you think there is more upside potential."
The survey showed allocations upticked modestly for certain European high-yield markets and cash.
